findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] NTScore — the model's per-nucleotide confidence: the conditional log-probability MIRTO assigns to the nucleotide actually present at a position when that position is masked and the rest of the transcript plus the encoded protein are given as context. Higher = the model thinks that exact base is strongly required by its context. Range in real data is roughly -4 to 0 (SOX2 3'UTR: mean -1.196, min -3.984, max -0.045).
findings.evidence: Manuscript Methods: 'The per-nucleotide score, NTScore, is defined as the conditional log-probability the model assigns to each observed nucleotide when that position is masked and all other tokens are provided as context, NTScore(i) = log P(x_i | x_{-i}).' Results: 'A higher NTScore indicates a nucleotide is of higher confidence and more strongly supported by the conditioning context from the model.' Measured with /opt/anaconda3/envs/bio/bin/python on /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/data/outputs_utr3_score_0318.h5 key NM_003106/score.
findings.portal_relevance: This is the single most important tooltip in the portal — every sequence track, the motif definition and the design story all sit on it. Must also carry the manuscript's own hedge (see CAVEAT entry) that it is a statistical likelihood, not a measured function.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] SeqScore — the mean NTScore over a whole named region (5'UTR, CDS or 3'UTR); a one-number 'how model-typical is this region'. Used to rank transcripts and to rank designed UTRs.
findings.evidence: Manuscript Methods: 'The sequence/region score (SeqScore) is the mean NTScore over a specified region (5' UTR, CDS or 3' UTR).' Fig 2c legend: '5'- and 3'-UTR SeqScores were computed and binned to 10 windows.'
findings.portal_relevance: Gene page needs a per-region SeqScore badge; it is trivially derivable from the two NTScore HDF5 files (mean of the score array) and needs no new computation.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] SpecScore — SeqScore minus the SeqScore of a composition-matched shuffled version of the same sequence, so a sequence cannot score well just by being A-rich or repetitive. Used only in the design workflow (Fig 5/6), not in motif discovery.
findings.evidence: Manuscript Methods: 'For sequence design, a specificity score (SpecScore) was defined as SeqScore minus the SeqScore of a composition-matched shuffled control, penalizing scores driven primarily by biased composition or repeats.' Thresholds used: 'SeqScore >= -1.01, SpecScore >= 0.39 and predicted stability >= 0.206' (top 1.65%).
findings.portal_relevance: Only needed if the portal surfaces the SOX2 design story. Keep it out of the motif/module glossary to avoid confusing visitors — it belongs to a different figure.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Delta-attention — the protein-to-UTR attention matrix computed on the real transcript MINUS the attention matrix computed on the same transcript with its UTR nucleotides masked. The subtraction removes positional and background attention bias; pooling the residual along each axis gives one importance profile for the protein and one for the UTR. Motif instances are where delta-attention peaks AND NTScore is high.
findings.evidence: Manuscript Methods: 'a null attention matrix, computed for the same transcript after masking its UTR nucleotides, was subtracted from the observed protein-UTR attention matrix to reduce positional and background-attention biases. Then projecting the resulting matrix along either axis produced separate importance profiles... These profiles were combined with high-confidence regions identified by NTScore to localize protein and UTR sequence features.'
findings.portal_relevance: This is the definition that makes a 'motif' in this portal different from a PWM hit in ATtRACT/RBPmap. The portal must say the motif is a MODEL ATTRIBUTION, not a database match. NOTE: no delta-attention matrices exist on disk (see GAPS) — Fig 3a is drawn from synthetic data.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Four nested motif objects the UI must keep distinct: (1) motif INSTANCE = one row in the master table = one substring in one transcript's one region (889,215 rows; utr3 515,752 / protein 254,466 / utr5 118,997); (2) unique_motif_id = a de-duplicated motif identity string, e.g. prot0145598, 577,186 distinct; (3) motif_cluster = the k-means group of motif embeddings, 900 total (prot_XXXX 300 / utr5_XXXX 100 / utr3_XXXX 500), from 500 kmeans_label values; (4) consensus / cid = a STREME-derived consensus string inside a cluster, addressed as cluster#index (e.g. utr5_0090#0), 1,226 of them across 516 clusters.
findings.evidence: Master table /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/sequence_annotation/sequence_annotation_human/data/processed/motif_full_annotations.parquet: 889,215 rows, columns raw_motif_index/unique_motif_id/kmeans_label/motif_cluster; verified 900 distinct motif_cluster. consensus_meta.csv at .../figure3_4/motif_pair_network/intermediate/ = 1,226 rows with columns cid,cluster,module,region,consensus,coverage,carriers. Manuscript Methods: 'By clustering these motif embeddings, they are aggregated into 900 clusters (300 protein, 100 5' UTR and 500 3' UTR clusters), obtained by k-means within each region. Per-cluster consensus logos were derived with STREME (MEME Suite, v5.5.9) against length- and region-matched background.'
findings.portal_relevance: R2 ('for a motif, show its cluster') hinges entirely on this hierarchy. A visitor clicking a highlighted stretch on a gene page is clicking an INSTANCE; its cluster is a k-means bucket; the consensus logo they then see is a STREME motif fitted to that bucket, and the instance need not match the consensus. The UI must say so or scientists will read the logo as the instance's own motif.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] coverage and carriers (per consensus) — 'carriers' = how many genes in the cluster contain that consensus; 'coverage' = the fraction of the cluster's member sequences that STREME matched with it. Coverage is often well below 1, i.e. the consensus describes only part of its own cluster. Examples: prot_0122#0 LLLLLL coverage 0.698 / 415 carriers; utr5_0090#0 GCCGCCGCCGC coverage 0.361 / 100 carriers; utr5_0004#0 CGCCGCCACC coverage 0.212 / only 51 carriers.
findings.evidence: consensus_meta.csv, columns coverage and carriers, read with pandas; values quoted verbatim from the rows for prot_0122, utr5_0090, utr5_0004.
findings.portal_relevance: Directly prevents over-reading. If a node's logo is shown at full size but its coverage is 0.21, the portal must show '21% of cluster members' next to it. This is exactly the number a reviewer will ask for and it is already computed.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] NPMI (normalized pointwise mutual information) — a co-occurrence score between one protein-motif cluster and one UTR-motif cluster, computed over binary per-gene presence across 18,068 human genes; NPMI(A,B) = log[P(A,B)/(P(A)P(B))] / -log P(A,B). It is 1 when the two always co-occur and 0 when independent.
findings.evidence: MODULES_REPORT.md at /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/sequence_analysis_v4_0621/03.interacting_modules/MODULES_REPORT.md: 'NPMI(A,B) = log[ P(A,B) / (P(A)·P(B)) ] / −log P(A,B) , P(·) = (#genes) / 18,068'. Manuscript Methods: 'quantified across human transcripts with normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) and average-product correction (APC), on binary per-transcript motif-cluster presence over 18,068 human genes.'
findings.portal_relevance: The edge weight in the R3 network. The unit is the GENE, not the molecule — an edge means 'these two motif clusters tend to appear in the same gene', which is the crux of the honesty problem.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] APC / MIp correction — subtracts each cluster's average association with everything else, so a promiscuous cluster (one that co-occurs with many partners simply because it is common) does not generate spurious strong edges. The corrected column is npmi_mip_APC and it, not npmi_raw, is the only NPMI-like quantity ever thresholded.
findings.evidence: protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv columns npmi_raw and npmi_mip_APC (180,000 rows). MODULES_REPORT.md: 'Did we threshold the NPMI values? Not the raw NPMI. A raw-NPMI cutoff would re-select the ZNF artifacts — they have the highest raw NPMI (≈0.90).'
findings.portal_relevance: If the portal exposes a sortable edge table it MUST default-sort on npmi_mip_APC or phylo_corrected_score. Sorting on npmi_raw reproduces the exact failure mode the authors spent the analysis correcting.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Phylogenetic-independence filter — a four-condition gate that an association must pass, all simultaneously: clade_concentration < 0.35 (no single protein family supplies >35% of the co-occurring genes), n_indep_clades >= 8 (at least 8 independent protein families carry both motifs), npmi_mip_APC > 0.10, and co_count >= 10. 2,620 of 166,615 co-occurring pairs pass.
findings.evidence: MODULES_REPORT.md table of four conditions, verbatim. Verified: protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv has 180,000 rows of which 166,615 have co_count>0 and exactly 2,620 have passes_phylo_filter==True; phylo_corrected_candidates.csv has 2,620 data rows. Protein families defined in Methods: 'a protein-sequence relatedness embedding built from their character 5-mer term frequency-Inverse document frequency (TF-IDF). Truncated SVD (256 dimensions) and Louvain community detection clustering was performed, giving 36 protein classes.'
findings.portal_relevance: This is the portal's headline credibility claim and should be a first-class UI object: every edge detail panel should show its four gate values so a reviewer can see WHY it passed. All four columns already exist per pair.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] phylo_corrected_score — the edge weight actually used for network layout: MIp x (1 - clade_concentration) x log1p(n_indep_clades). High when the association is specific, spread across many families, and not driven by one expanded family. 0 for every pair that fails the gate.
findings.evidence: MODULES_REPORT.md: 'Edge weight = phylo_corrected_score = MIp × (1 − clade_concentration) × log1p(n_indep_clades)'. Column present in protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv and phylo_corrected_candidates.csv; top value observed 1.7694 for prot_0040 x utr5_0004.
findings.portal_relevance: Use as edge thickness in the R3 view; expose the formula in a tooltip so the thickness is interpretable rather than decorative.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Module (M1–M6) — a Louvain community of the bipartite graph whose nodes are protein-motif and UTR-motif clusters and whose edges are the 2,620 gated pairs. Louvain gave modularity 0.47 and 9 communities; the 6 retained ones each have >=2 protein motifs, >=2 UTR motifs and >=3 edges. Module names (TF, extracellular, immune, RNA-processing, translation/histone) come from POST-HOC GO enrichment, not from the clustering.
findings.evidence: MODULES_REPORT.md: 'Louvain (community_multilevel, seeded → reproducible): modularity 0.47, 9 communities. Keep communities with ≥2 protein motifs, ≥2 UTR motifs, ≥3 edges → the 6 modules' and 'Modules from interaction structure (bipartite communities); GO computed afterwards as an independent readout'. Verified from modules.json: M1 39x67 774 edges, M2 39x73 409, M3 62x71 385, M4 20x53 123, M5 24x33 126, M6 14x18 43.
findings.portal_relevance: The R3 'meta modules' view IS this object. Note the naming provenance: labelling a node 'immune module' is a GO summary of the member genes, not a property of the motifs.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Carrier gene / module gene member — a gene is a member of module M if and only if it carries BOTH motifs (the protein motif AND the UTR motif) of at least one gated pair belonging to M. Counts: M1 3,388, M2 3,046, M3 4,348, M4 1,988, M5 1,607, M6 1,562; genes matching at least one significant GO term of their module: 3,083 / 2,434 / 3,112 / 844 / 1,482 / 1,390.
findings.evidence: module_gene_members/README.md at /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/sequence_analysis_v4_0621/03.interacting_modules/: 'a gene is a member of module M iff it carries both motifs (the protein motif AND the UTR motif) of at least one gated pair belonging to M' plus the per-module counts table, verbatim.
findings.portal_relevance: 'Carrier' at the CONSENSUS level is a different, much smaller number (e.g. 13 genes carry prot_0122#0 AND utr5_0090#0 vs 4,348 genes in M3). The portal will confuse people unless it labels the two levels differently — suggest 'module member' vs 'motif-pair carrier'.

findings.claim: [GLOSSARY] Trusted (leading) term — the stricter GO subset the authors actually report: FDR q<0.05 AND fold enrichment >=2 AND supported by >=5 independent paralog families. A term inflated by one expanded family is excluded. Trusted counts: M1 1,419 of 2,310 significant; M2 442/962; M3 383/926; M4 223/342; M5 593/1,086; M6 470/763.
findings.evidence: module_gene_members/README.md: 'Trusted (leading) term — a stricter subset: q<0.05 and fold≥2 and n_fam_support≥5 independent paralog families. These are the family-unbiased themes... a term inflated by one expanded paralog family is excluded.' Counts read from module_leading_terms.csv columns n_sig / n_trusted.

Arrive with: (Q1) 'Is this just paralog-family structure re-labelled as biology?' → answer with the raw-top-30 verdict table, the four gate values on every edge, mean_frac_ZNF per module (M1 0.062, M2 0.042, M3 0.003, M4 0.027, M5 0.014, M6 0.002) and the Meff 2342/18068 number. (Q2) 'Does a specific figure claim hold when I look at the underlying genes?' → answer with clickable carrier gene sets behind every panel (13 M3 genes, 49 M5 genes, 17 M6 histones, 372 Kozak genes). (Q3) 'What is a motif here, operationally?' → answer with the delta-attention + NTScore definition, the instance/cluster/consensus hierarchy, and per-cluster coverage.

findings.claim: [AUDIENCE 2 — RNA-biology wet-lab readers]. Arrive with: (Q1) 'Does MY gene have anything?' → the R1 gene page: 5'UTR/3'UTR/protein sequence with highlighted motifs and the NTScore track. Median gene has 21 3'UTR motifs, 11 protein motifs and 5 5'UTR motifs (means 28.5 / 14.1 / 6.6; 3'UTR max 182), so the highlight layer needs density controls from day one. (Q2) 'Which RBP might bind here?' → the four CLIP columns per instance plus the cluster's eCLIP enrichment with fold/k/n. (Q3) 'Is this element known or new?' → InterPro/UniProt/MobiDB/ELM for protein, TargetScan for 3'UTR, with coverage% shown.

findings.claim: [AUDIENCE 3 — mRNA design engineers]. Arrive with: (Q1) 'Given my protein, which UTR motifs should I include?' → the R3 module view read backwards: find the protein motif cluster matching your protein's domains (InterPro labels on prot_ nodes), follow its gated edges to UTR clusters, read their consensus. (Q2) 'What does a good UTR look like by this model?' → SeqScore/SpecScore and the SOX2 design case with real thresholds (SeqScore ≥ -1.01, SpecScore ≥ 0.39, stability ≥ 0.206; top 1.65%) and measured outcomes (U7 nuclear fraction 54.6±5.2% vs α-globin 17.5±0.8%, 3.1-fold, P=5.2e-11; U3 NANOG 2.1-fold, P=2.7e-5; FL1 74.99±6.67% nuclear vs 18.35±4.00%, 4.09-fold, P=4.9e-9). (Q3) 'Will this generalise to my cell type?' → the answer is no and the manuscript says so: 'the current conditioning variables do not explicitly represent cell type, developmental state, delivery route or disease context.'
findings.evidence: Manuscript Results (SOX2 design numbers, verbatim) and Methods (selection thresholds, verbatim); Discussion limitations, verbatim.
findings.portal_relevance: This audience will try to use the motif table as a design rulebook. The portal should make the direction of inference explicit — the motifome is descriptive of endogenous human transcripts; the design claims come from a separate generative workflow validated on ONE protein in ONE primary cell type.

findings.claim: [PRIOR ART] The interaction patterns worth copying from this genre, with the specific reason each fits: (a) ATtRACT / RBPmap — a 'scan any sequence' box returning ranked PWM hits with a score and a p/q value; copy the idea of a per-hit score column, but MIRTO motifs are attribution regions not PWM scans, so a scan box would misrepresent the method. (b) oRNAment — per-transcript RBP-site tracks broken out by region (5'UTR/CDS/3'UTR) with a region selector; this is almost exactly requirement R1 and its region-tab pattern is the right skeleton. (c) POSTAR3 — CLIP peaks from many methods stacked as separate tracks with the method named on each; the master table already has four separate CLIP columns (eCLIP, PAR-CLIP/PARalyzer, iCLIP/Piranha_0.01, iCLIP/CIMS) and should stack them the same way rather than merging into one 'RBP' field. (d) InterPro / UniProt feature viewer — a horizontal protein bar with stacked domain/feature tracks and hover detail; directly reusable for the protein half of R1, with plddt as an extra track. (e) TargetScan — showing conservation and context score next to every site so the user can triage; the analogue here is motif_score + NTScore + coverage. (f) ENCODE portal — faceted search with visible result counts on every facet; the right model for browsing 900 clusters and 2,620 pairs.
findings.evidence: No web access was used; this is from model knowledge of these resources and is therefore UNCERTAIN in detail (exact current UI of any of these sites may differ). The mapping to this project's columns is verified: the four CLIP list columns and plddt exist in motif_full_annotations.parquet as listed.
findings.portal_relevance: Concrete UI skeleton: region-tabbed sequence viewer (oRNAment) + stacked method-labelled annotation tracks (POSTAR3) + protein feature bar (InterPro) + faceted counts (ENCODE).

findings.claim: [PRIOR ART] Pitfalls specific to this genre that this project is unusually exposed to: (a) motif-atlas portals routinely present a PWM logo as if it were the site found in the user's gene — here that is actively wrong because the consensus is a STREME fit to a k-means bucket with coverage as low as 0.21; (b) network views make co-occurrence look like binding — the manuscript's own limitation language must be on-screen; (c) portals that let users sort by the rawest available score reproduce the artifact the analysis removed (raw NPMI top-30 is 25/30 ZNF artifact); (d) 'gene not found' is a common dead end — 1,117 transcripts in the sequence table have zero motifs and 246 gene symbols in the motif table have no unique symbol match, so an empty-state design is mandatory; (e) resources that show only supporting statistics erode trust with expert readers — several of this project's own tables contain non-significant results (APEX lamina q=0.725, OMM q=0.551; four of seven M5 kinetics metrics ns for the 'both' group) and showing them is a net gain.
findings.evidence: Coverage 0.212 for utr5_0004#0 from consensus_meta.csv; RAW_top30_annotated.csv verdict counts; computed set difference: 1,117 transcripts in GRCh37_latest_rna_sequence_pairs_long_transcript.parquet have no row in the motif table, and 18,093 sequence_ids map to 17,847 unique gene_symbols; q-values from m1_m2_apex_localization.csv and motif_2x2_kinetics_summary.csv. Genre pitfalls themselves are model knowledge and UNCERTAIN.
findings.portal_relevance: Each pitfall maps to a specific, cheap UI decision that should be made before the first line of code rather than retrofitted.

gaps.gap: MANUSCRIPT-vs-DATA CONFLICT: the manuscript says 'MLXIPL ... contains the M2 utr3_0027 motifs (Fig. 4a)', but every data file assigns utr3_0027 to MODULE 1, and the figure code that actually built Fig 4a uses utr3_0227 (module 2). This looks like a one-character typo in the manuscript (0027 vs 0227).
gaps.impact: If the portal is built from the data it will contradict the published sentence on the flagship M2 example; if built from the sentence it will show a module-1 cluster labelled M2. Either way a reviewer who checks will find an inconsistency, and this is the one example gene the manuscript names for M2.
gaps.workaround: Confirmed evidence for the typo reading: modules.json maps utr3_0027->module 1 and utr3_0227->module 2; consensus_meta.csv, cluster_term_labels.csv and utr_composition.csv all independently say utr3_0027 module=1; examples_of_each_gene/MLXIPL_M2_signatures.csv and build_mlxipl_signatures.py both use utr3_0227; m1_m2_gene_assignment.csv gives MLXIPL n_m1_utr=0, n_m2_utr=7, lean=M2. Ask the author to confirm, then build on utr3_0227 and consider an erratum note. (Note utr3_0027's composition is fC=0.484, GC=0.533 — genuinely C-rich, which is why it reads as an M2-style cluster even though Louvain put it in M1.)

gaps.gap: No per-nucleotide score exists for the CDS or the protein. The two NTScore HDF5 caches cover 5'UTR and 3'UTR only.

gaps.gap: No delta-attention matrices are stored anywhere on disk. Fig 3a is drawn from synthetic data.
gaps.impact: The portal cannot show a visitor the actual attribution that defined a motif — the one thing that would fully explain 'why is this stretch highlighted'.

gaps.gap: One transcript per gene only. The motif table has 18,093 sequence_ids and 17,847 unique gene symbols — essentially the longest isoform per gene — and the sequence table likewise. There is no isoform-level motifome.
gaps.impact: The CD47/CD44 story in the manuscript is entirely about long- vs short-3'UTR ISOFORMS producing the same protein. A generic gene search for CD47 returns only NM_001777 (3'UTR 4,197 nt) with no short isoform to compare against, so the portal cannot let a user reproduce the paper's own isoform argument. Same limitation for any alternative-UTR question a visitor brings.

gaps.gap: The sequence table has duplicate keys: 21,667 rows but only 19,210 unique refseq_id_without_ver values (2,457 duplicate rows, from multiple Ensembl transcript mappings per RefSeq ID).
gaps.impact: A naive .set_index('refseq_id_without_ver') lookup returns a Series instead of a string and silently breaks sequence slicing — this actually happened during verification.
gaps.workaround: drop_duplicates('refseq_id_without_ver') before indexing. Build the portal's serving layer from a deduplicated table keyed on RefSeq ID, and keep the Ensembl mappings in a separate one-to-many side table if cross-links are wanted.

gaps.gap: Alphabet mismatch between layers: motif instances and UTR sequences are stored in the DNA alphabet (T), while every STREME consensus string is in the RNA alphabet (U). E.g. the utr3_0463 consensus is 'UCUUUU' but the instance substring is 'TCTTTT'.
gaps.impact: Any string comparison, highlight-matching or search box that does not normalise will silently fail to match consensus to instance, and users typing 'UCUCC' will get zero hits.
gaps.workaround: Verified: motifs column for utr3 rows contains 'T' and never 'U'. Normalise both directions in the search index and display UTR sequences as RNA (U) throughout the UI for scientific correctness, while matching on a T-normalised key.

recommendations: RESOLVE THE utr3_0027 / utr3_0227 CONFLICT WITH THE AUTHOR BEFORE BUILDING ANYTHING. The manuscript's only named M2 example ('MLXIPL ... contains the M2 utr3_0027 motifs') contradicts modules.json (utr3_0027 -> M1) while the code that produced that very figure uses utr3_0227 (-> M2). All evidence points to a typo, but the portal will publicly expose the inconsistency on its M2 landing card either way. This is a one-question email and it blocks the M2 example.

MAKE THE INSTANCE / CLUSTER / CONSENSUS HIERARCHY AN EXPLICIT UI CONTROL, NOT AN IMPLICIT ONE. The same question ('which genes carry this motif pair?') returns 4,348 / 49 / 15 genes at module, cluster and consensus resolution. Give the user a visible resolution selector and always print which level the current number came from. This single decision prevents most of the misreading risk in R2 and R3, and all three levels are already computable from files on disk.

BUILD THE SEQUENCE VIEWER AROUND THE NTScore TRACK, NOT AROUND COLOURED TEXT. The two HDF5 caches give a per-nucleotide score whose length matches the region sequence exactly for all 18,093 transcripts (verified on six genes, all exact). A gene page showing sequence + score track + motif spans + CLIP/miRNA annotation lanes is a genuinely new object for this field; coloured letters alone would be a worse version of what oRNAment already does. Accept the asymmetry that the protein panel has no track and use plddt as its analogue.

LEAD WITH THE prot_0040 x utr5_0004 KOZAK EDGE AS THE DEFAULT R3 ENTRY POINT. It is the top-scoring pair in the analysis (phylo_corrected_score 1.7694, co_count 175, n_indep_clades 23, frac_co_ZNF 0.0), its UTR consensus is CGCCGCCACC, its protein cluster is histone-fold at InterPro fold 26.45, its sibling edge utr3_0463 shows SLBP enrichment at fold 48.6 on 17 histone genes, and 372 carrier genes are pre-classified by Kozak strength. A visitor who watches the method independently rediscover the Kozak sequence and the histone stem-loop will trust everything else on the site.

SHIP THE 'WHY WE CORRECTED FOR PARALOGY' PAGE AS A FIRST-CLASS VIEW, NOT A FOOTNOTE. RAW_top30_annotated.csv (30 rows, 4 KB, with a human-written verdict column showing 25/30 are ZNF clade artifacts), independent_origins.csv, cmh_family_stratified_highlight.csv and relatedness_report.md (Meff 2,342 of 18,068; ZNF 547 -> effective 9.0) together make the most persuasive case in the entire project. Every edge detail panel should also show its four gate values (clade_concentration, n_indep_clades, npmi_mip_APC, co_count) against their thresholds.

DEFAULT-SORT EVERY EDGE TABLE ON phylo_corrected_score OR npmi_mip_APC AND DO NOT EXPOSE npmi_raw AS A SORT KEY WITHOUT A WARNING. Sorting on raw NPMI regenerates exactly the artifact leaderboard the analysis removed — this is the single most likely way for the portal to embarrass the paper.

RENDER CROSS-MODULE EDGES IN THE R3 VIEW. 757 of the 2,620 gated pairs (28.9%) connect different modules, and the manuscript itself highlights the M1<->M5 link (192 edges) as biologically meaningful. A view that only draws within-module edges silently discards nearly a third of the result and loses the one cross-module observation the paper makes.

DISTINGUISH TWO BADGE CLASSES ON EVERY NODE: 'evidence in this dataset' (an eCLIP/InterPro/MobiDB enrichment with its fold, k and n from cluster_term_labels.csv) versus 'author inference from literature' (a resemblance the manuscript proposes, e.g. utr5_0096 ~ SRSF3/4, utr3_0215 ~ PTBP, neither of which has an enrichment row in the data). Carry the manuscript's own hedge on the second class verbatim: 'although their direct binding and function in this module remain to be experimentally established.'

SHOW NON-SIGNIFICANT RESULTS ALONGSIDE SIGNIFICANT ONES ON EVERY VALIDATION PANEL. The APEX table has lamina q=0.725 and OMM q=0.551 despite the manuscript sentence claiming both; the M5 2x2 has four of seven metrics ns for the 'both' group. Displaying all rows with their q-values costs nothing, pre-empts the reviewer's own check, and makes the two genuinely strong effects (PUND 1.9%->15.6%, polysome t1/2 9.9->3.4 min) more credible rather than less.

PRECOMPUTE PER-GENE JSON SHARDS AT BUILD TIME; DO NOT QUERY PARQUET AT REQUEST TIME. Raw inputs exceed 300 MB. Emit one shard per gene (sequence, motif spans, downsampled NTScore, annotations, module fingerprint) plus small global tables (900 clusters, 2,620 edges, 6 modules, 1,226 consensuses, 65 cluster labels). Use the verified coordinate contract: motif_start/motif_end are 0-based INCLUSIVE on both ends (slice [start:end+1]), confirmed exact on 20,000/20,000 sampled rows and motif_length == end-start+1 for all 889,215 rows. Deduplicate the sequence table on refseq_id_without_ver (21,667 rows -> 19,210 unique) before indexing, and normalise T/U between the DNA-alphabet instance strings and the RNA-alphabet consensus strings.

DESIGN FOR MOTIF DENSITY AND FOR EMPTY STATES FROM THE START. The median gene carries 21 3'UTR motifs (mean 28.5, max 182) plus 11 protein and 5 5'UTR motifs, and 45.3% of instances belong to clusters with no module. Ship filter chips (by module / by score / by annotated-only) and a proper 'no module assigned' presentation on day one; also handle the 1,117 transcripts with zero motifs and the 246 gene symbols that do not map one-to-one.

ASK THE AUTHOR TWO SCOPE QUESTIONS THAT MATERIALLY CHANGE THE BUILD: (1) Should the portal include the SOX2 design story (Fig 5/6) or stay purely descriptive? It is a different audience (mRNA engineers) and a different data tree (sequence_design/sox2_full_length/). (2) Should mouse be included? A parallel 827,161-instance annotated mouse motifome exists (identified_motifs_with_clusters_mouse_0601.parquet, GRCm39 sequences, mouse coverage stats) and would enable the cross-species PTP4A2 story, but mouse annotation coverage is far lower (any-annotation 25.3% vs 63.9% human) and it roughly doubles the build.

Warm-cache timings (min of 5): SELECT * WHERE gene_symbol='TP53' on the original 1-row-group file = 78.3 ms; on B_sorted_rg8000 = 7.3 ms. Cluster query (motif_cluster='utr3_0215', 566 rows): 155.4 ms vs 72.3 ms. On the untouched 24-column original the same gene query took 125.5 ms all-columns and 33.9 ms for a 6-column projection.
findings.portal_relevance: Confirms a FastAPI/Flask backend over the re-partitioned parquet answers R1 gene lookups in single-digit ms, with no database server to maintain.

findings.claim: Per-gene static JSON shards are ~50x cheaper per query than even the optimally re-partitioned parquet, and are tiny.
findings.evidence: Built all 17,847 real shards (gene -> all its motifs + all 11 annotation fields, gzip -9) in 44.8 s. Total 46.61 MB logical; median 2,369 B, p90 4,398 B, p99 6,251 B, max 11,301 B. Actual `du` = 81.0 MB because 17,847 small files pad to 4 KB blocks. Prototypes at .../scratchpad/sizing/gene_shards/
findings.portal_relevance: R1 (search a gene) costs a 2.4 KB fetch at the median and 11.3 KB in the absolute worst case. This makes a fully static, zero-backend portal the natural default for R1.

findings.claim: Motif instances NEVER overlap within a (transcript, region), so sequence highlighting needs only a single flat track — no stacking, no interval tree.
findings.evidence: Computed max interval depth via a heap sweep over 4,000 transcripts' 3'UTR motif sets: max overlap depth p50=1, p90=1, p99=1, MAX=1; fraction of transcripts with any overlapping 3'UTR motifs = 0.000. Merged-interval count equals raw motif count exactly (p50 21, max 182).
findings.portal_relevance: The R1 sequence viewer is dramatically simpler than a typical genome browser track: one row per region, motifs are a disjoint partition of the sequence.

findings.claim: The '8,000 nt 3'UTR' worst case is real but rare, and segment-based rendering keeps every gene page under 400 elements.
findings.evidence: Over the 18,093 transcripts that actually carry motifs: utr3 p50=1,062 nt, p90=3,661, p95=4,549, p99=6,008, p99.9=7,031, MAX=7,601 nt. Only 587 transcripts (3.2%) have utr3 >= 5,000 nt and only 23 (0.1%) >= 7,000 nt. utr5 p50=186 / max 4,705; protein p50=401 aa / max 3,695 aa. Element counts for a page showing all three sequences: one-element-per-residue gives p50=1,940, p99=6,809, MAX=7,784 (worst gene NM_001351027); one-element-per-motif-or-gap-segment gives p50=89, p99=279, MAX=381 (worst NM_001003665). Zero genes exceed 10,000 per-nt elements; zero exceed 1,000 segments.
findings.portal_relevance: Even the naive per-nucleotide DOM approach never exceeds ~7.8k nodes, which modern browsers handle. But segment spans are 24x cheaper at p99 and are the obvious choice. 3'UTR max wraps to 127 lines at 60 nt/line.

findings.claim: The R3 module network is small enough for plain SVG + d3-force; only the Fig 3c UMAP needs canvas/WebGL.
findings.evidence: modules.json: 6 modules totalling 513 nodes / 1,860 edges (M1 106n/774e, M2 112n/409e, M3 133n/385e, M4 73n/123e, M5 57n/126e, M6 32n/43e). Densest is M1 at 0.296 of bipartite max. The full passing set is 2,620 edges over 519 nodes; 760 passing edges fall outside all six modules. The unfiltered pair space is 180,000 edges over 900 nodes. The figure-selected subset bipartite_nodes_all6.csv is only 52 nodes.
findings.portal_relevance: 513/1,860 is comfortably inside SVG+force-layout territory. The 180,000-point UMAP is not, and needs a canvas or WebGL scatter.

findings.claim: The Fig 3c UMAP coordinates already exist as a cached array and compress to under 1 MB as a binary payload.
findings.evidence: /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/sequence_analysis_v3_0515/07.umap_vis/00.build_embeddings_model_embeddings/results/cca_sweep/cca_winner_umap.npy is (180000, 2) float32; row_index.csv is (180000, 11) with columns row, pair_id, go_key, protein, utr, utr_end, protein_row, utr_row. Merging onto protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv on (protein, utr) keeps 180,000/180,000. Encodings: float32 raw 1.440 MB (gz 1.330); uint16 quantized xy 0.720 MB (gz 0.713) with max quantization error 0.000234 data units over a 27.5x30.3 bbox; uint16 npmi channel gz 0.266 MB; uint8 module channel gz 0.014 MB. Total interactive payload gz = 0.994 MB, vs 4.878 MB as JSON records (4.9x smaller). Only 11,966/180,000 points belong to a module.
findings.portal_relevance: An interactive Fig 3c is a ~1 MB typed-array download plus a canvas scatter. No recomputation needed.

findings.claim: Full-table JSON is not viable; columnar or sharded encodings are 7-12x smaller.
findings.evidence: Extrapolated from a real 20,000-row sample of the 889,215-row master table: JSON records 568.97 MB raw / 80.78 MB gzip; NDJSON identical (568.97 / 80.78); columnar JSON (arrays per column) 257.13 MB / 47.10 MB gzip. A 9-column slim projection: 168.88 MB JSON / 28.93 MB gzip, or 11.36 MB as zstd-9 parquet / 15.43 MB snappy parquet.
findings.portal_relevance: Rules out shipping the master table as one JSON blob. Parquet at 11.4 MB (zstd) or per-gene shards at 46.6 MB total are the real options.

findings.claim: DuckDB's native file format is larger than parquet and buys nothing for a static deployment.
findings.evidence: CREATE TABLE from the 44.5 MB source parquet then CHECKPOINT: 52.97 MB with no indexes, 78.92 MB after adding indexes on gene_symbol and motif_cluster. Indexed gene query 5.2 ms.
findings.portal_relevance: For a server-backed deployment use parquet + DuckDB's parquet reader, not a materialized .duckdb file. The 5.2 ms indexed number only matters for option (c)/(d).

findings.claim: An in-memory pandas app server needs ~800 MB RAM for the master table alone, which excludes most free tiers.
findings.evidence: pq.read_table(motif_full_annotations.parquet).to_pandas() -> df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() = 782.2 MB for 889,215 x 24. Read time 0.84 s. The sequence table adds 109.4 MB (21,667 x 13).
findings.portal_relevance: Streamlit Community Cloud (~1 GB) and small container tiers will OOM if the app naively loads the full table. Either query parquet lazily via DuckDB (which streams) or preload only the 11.4 MB slim projection.

findings.claim: The transcript sequence table contains 1,296 duplicated RefSeq IDs, and every duplicate group is byte-identical, so dedup is lossless and mandatory.
findings.evidence: refseq_id_without_ver has 19,210 distinct values across 21,667 rows; 1,296 IDs occur more than once (NM_153443 appears 42 times, NM_006737 34x, NM_014218 33x). Grouping by refseq_id_without_ver: 0 of 1,296 duplicate groups have more than one distinct utr3_sequence, and 0 have more than one distinct protein_sequence. The 42 NM_153443 rows map to 42 different Gene stable IDs (ENSG00000242019, ENSG00000273502, ...) with identical transcript_length 1001.
findings.portal_relevance: drop_duplicates(subset='refseq_id_without_ver') is safe and takes the join from 20,481 matched rows down to the correct 18,093. Skipping this silently duplicates motif tracks in the R1 view.

findings.claim: Join keys between motif and sequence tables are clean: refseq_id_without_ver and best_refseq_mrna_id both cover 100% of motif transcripts; the Ensembl key covers 0%.
findings.evidence: Overlap of the 18,093 distinct motif sequence_id values against sequence-table columns: refseq_id_without_ver 18,093/18,093, best_refseq_mrna_id 18,093/18,093, 'RefSeq mRNA ID' 16,476/18,093, transcript_stable_id 0/18,093.
findings.portal_relevance: Use refseq_id_without_ver as the canonical join key. Do not use transcript_stable_id or the versioned 'RefSeq mRNA ID' column.

findings.claim: Per-transcript sequence shards are even smaller than motif shards.
findings.evidence: Built 20,481 real shards {id, utr5, utr3, prot} gzip -9: total 20.08 MB, p50 850 B, p90 1,804 B, p99 2,501 B, max 2,720 B; du 71 MB (block padding). Scaled to the 18,093 usable transcripts = 17.74 MB. Whole-table alternatives: 47.88 MB JSON / 17.64 MB gzip / 15.41 MB zstd parquet / 26.97 MB snappy parquet. Total sequence characters across utr5+utr3+protein = 45.85 M.
findings.portal_relevance: R1 needs two fetches totalling ~3.2 KB at the median (2,369 B motif shard + 850 B sequence shard).

findings.claim: Per-cluster shards cover R2 at 900 files and modest size.
findings.evidence: Built all 900 real shards (cluster -> every member motif instance with annotations, gzip -9): total 41.98 MB, p50 43,770 B, p90 69,607 B, max 217,326 B. Motifs per cluster: p50 920, p99 2,387, max 5,755 (utr3_0188), min 218.
findings.portal_relevance: R2 costs a 43.8 KB fetch at the median, 217 KB worst case. Acceptable, but large clusters should paginate their member table rather than render 5,755 rows.

findings.claim: The whole R3 network layer is 1.4-7.5 MB gzipped depending on how much of the pair space ships.
findings.evidence: Gzipped-JSON sizes measured per product: protein_utr_FINAL_scores 180,000x15 = 5.401 MB (but only 1.93 MB if trimmed to 9 key columns); consensus_pair_scores 49,547x13 = 0.690 MB (only 0.027 MB if restricted to the 1,266 passing rows); module_term_gene_lists 0.602; module_gene_index 12,345x8 = 0.512; module_GO_enrichment 6,389x12 = 0.203; phylo_corrected_candidates 2,620x15 = 0.089; consensus_meta 1,226x7 = 0.018; cluster_term_labels 65x17 = 0.007; consensus_scope_clusters 513x3 = 0.002; modules.json = 0.0017; module_leading_terms, GO_term_specificity, RAW_top30, modules_summary, bipartite_nodes all <= 0.001. Sum of everything = 7.529 MB; lean variant (drop the 180k and 49.5k pair tables) = 1.438 MB.
findings.portal_relevance: R3 can land as a sub-1.5 MB first-class view and lazily pull the full 180k pair table only when the user opens the UMAP or an all-pairs explorer.

findings.claim: Total fully-static portal is ~114 MB gzipped; shell + lazy shards gives a 334 KB first paint.
findings.evidence: Summing the measured products: per-gene shards 46.61 + per-transcript sequence shards 17.74 + per-cluster shards 41.98 + full R3 layer 7.53 + search index 0.157 + app shell ~0.15 (the only estimated line) = 114.17 MB. Lean variant = 108.07 MB. Lazy-load first paint = shell 0.15 + search index 0.157 + modules.json 0.002 + consensus_meta 0.018 + cluster_term_labels 0.007 = 334 KB, or 423 KB if the 2,620-edge list loads eagerly. Per-action after that: gene lookup 3.2 KB median / 8.8 KB p99 / 14.0 KB max; cluster open 43.8 KB median / 217 KB max; module subgraph expand 89 KB.
findings.portal_relevance: 114 MB fits GitHub Pages' 1 GB soft repo limit and Netlify's free tier. The 334 KB first paint is excellent. The cost is ~36,700 small files in the repo, which makes git clone slow.

findings.claim: The gene search index is trivially small, and 215 genes need a transcript picker.
findings.evidence: gene_symbol -> (sequence_id, n_motifs) for all 17,847 genes = 0.91 MB JSON / 0.157 MB gzip. 17,632 genes have exactly 1 transcript; 193 have 2, 17 have 3, 3 have 4, 1 has 5, 1 has 7 (max). Zero sequence_ids map to more than one gene_symbol. Motifs per gene: p50 43, p90 93, p99 142, max 336 (CYFIP1).
findings.portal_relevance: Whole search index loads at first paint. R1 needs a transcript selector, but only for 215/17,847 genes (1.2%).

findings.claim: Annotation coverage reproduces the stated coverage_stats.json exactly when recomputed from the master table.
findings.evidence: Recomputed non-empty fractions over all 889,215 rows: MobIDB 48.57% overall / 87.21% of protein rows; uniprot 25.81% / 90.20% protein; interpro 19.39% / 67.76% protein; RBPs_PAR-CLIP,PARalyzer 29.57% / 41.42% UTR; RBPs_eCLIP 16.40% / 22.97% UTR; RBPs_iCLIP,CIMS 15.25% / 21.36% UTR; RBPs_iCLIP,Piranha 8.90% / 12.47% UTR; miRNA targetscan 2.73% / 3.82% UTR; idpo 0.42% / 0.75% protein; signalp 0.11% / 0.12% protein; elm 0.09% / 0.31% protein. ANY RBP evidence = 36.66% overall, 51.36% of UTR rows.
findings.portal_relevance: Confirms the 51.4% RBP / 67.8% InterPro / 90.2% UniProt figures. The UI must show 'no annotation' states as a first-class case, not an error, for roughly a third of all motifs.

findings.claim: Facet cardinalities for R2 filters are small and enumerable.
findings.evidence: Across all four CLIP sources there are 203 distinct RBP names; 219 distinct TargetScan miRNA families; 900 motif clusters; 500 kmeans labels; 3 regions.
findings.portal_relevance: Every filter dropdown fits in a client-side list. An inverted index RBP -> clusters/genes would be small enough to ship statically.

findings.claim: plddt is stored on a 0-1 scale, not 0-100, and motif_score is always negative.
findings.evidence: plddt over the 254,466 protein rows: min 0.1, p50 0.8, p99 1.0, max 1.0, mean 0.70. motif_score: min -4.831, p50 -1.135, p99 -0.02, max -0.0, mean -1.211. motif_entropy: min 0.0, p50 1.179, max 2.947.
findings.portal_relevance: Color legends and thresholds must use 0-1 for pLDDT (a naive 0-100 AlphaFold scale would render every motif as 'very low confidence') and a negative-valued scale for motif_score.

findings.claim: The existing HTML reports contain zero interactive code and cannot be extended into the portal, but the sequence-view plotting logic is reusable.
findings.evidence: grep for '<script' in 03.interacting_modules/MODULES_REPORT.html returns 0 matches; REPORT.html has no external script tags. Both are matplotlib PNGs base64-embedded into static markdown-rendered HTML by make_modules_html.py. Separately, examples_of_each_gene/examples_lib.py defines reusable helpers: region_of(cl), seqcol_of(cl), sid_for(symbol, cl), context(sid, cl, flank), go_terms(symbol, n), function(symbol, cl), aacol(a) (an amino-acid color scheme), msa_context_plot, msa_plot_fragments.
findings.portal_relevance: No JS to inherit. But region_of/seqcol_of/sid_for/context encode exactly the cluster-prefix -> region -> sequence-column -> coordinate-slice logic the R1 view needs, and aacol is an existing amino-acid palette to stay consistent with the manuscript figures.

gaps.gap: 387 of 900 motif clusters (43%) have no module assignment, so R2's 'how it interacts with protein features' is undefined for nearly half the motif space.
gaps.impact: 486,307 of 889,215 motif instances (54.7%) sit in a module-assigned cluster; the other 402,908 (45.3%) can show a cluster and its annotations but have no module context, no partner-cluster edges and no consensus. Region split of the 513 module clusters: protein 198/300, utr3 249/500, utr5 66/100 -- so 3'UTR and 5'UTR clusters are the worst covered.
gaps.workaround: Do not hide unassigned clusters. Give every cluster a page, and render a distinct explicit state: 'This cluster did not pass the phylogenetic-independence filter into any of the six modules.' Still show its NPMI partners from protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv (all 900 clusters appear there) with passes_phylo_filter=false rendered as greyed, clearly sub-threshold evidence.

gaps.gap: Only 37 of 900 clusters (4.1%) have a curated enrichment label in cluster_term_labels.csv, and the figure's bipartite node set is only 52 nodes.
gaps.impact: cluster_term_labels.csv has 65 rows covering 37 distinct clusters; bipartite_nodes_all6.csv has 52 nodes. The other 863 clusters would render with a bare ID like utr3_0188 and no human-readable name, which makes the R3 network mostly unlabelled if the portal relies on this file.
gaps.workaround: Derive labels for the remaining clusters at build time from the master table itself: top InterPro/UniProt term for protein clusters and top RBP by CLIP support for UTR clusters, both computable from motif_full_annotations.parquet. Mark these as auto-derived and visually distinguish them from the 37 curated labels. cluster_term_enrichment.csv.gz (13 MB) is the likely source for a broader auto-labelling pass.

gaps.gap: STREME consensus strings exist for only 451 of 900 clusters, and 62 clusters that ARE in a module still lack one.
gaps.impact: R3 explicitly asks for 'motif consensus' on the module view. consensus_meta.csv has 1,226 rows covering 451 clusters (mean 2.72 consensus strings each, max 10), scoped to the 513 module clusters. 62 module clusters have no consensus at all, and all 387 non-module clusters have none.
gaps.workaround: For clusters without a STREME consensus, compute a position frequency matrix directly from the member motif strings in the master table and render a sequence logo client-side. Motifs are short (p50 length 8 nt/aa) and clusters have 218-5,755 members, so this is cheap. Label logo provenance ('STREME' vs 'derived from member instances') so the manuscript figure and the portal never silently disagree.

gaps.gap: No stated hosting target, no git repo, and no CI anywhere in the task directory.
gaps.impact: /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/manuscript/online_contents contains only instructions/00.build_idea.md and an empty code/ dir. There is no deployment pipeline to extend and no decision on file-serving infrastructure, which is the single choice that most constrains the architecture.
gaps.workaround: Build the data-generation step as a standalone, idempotent Python script that emits a self-contained static directory. That artifact deploys unchanged to GitHub Pages, Netlify, a lab web server, or an S3 bucket, and can be zipped into a Zenodo deposit. Defer the hosting decision without blocking the build.

gaps.gap: DuckDB is not installed in any interpreter on this machine, so nothing in the current environment can execute the option-(b)/(c) query path as-is.
gaps.impact: All four candidate interpreters raise ModuleNotFoundError for duckdb. Any pipeline step or backend that assumes DuckDB will fail on a fresh checkout.
gaps.workaround: duckdb 1.5.5 installs cleanly via pip (verified). Pin it in a requirements.txt. Note that DuckDB is only needed for the re-partitioning build step and for a server-backed deployment; the fully static shard architecture needs pyarrow only, which is already present at version 21.0.0.

gaps.gap: Fig 3c UMAP coordinates live outside the documented data set, in a v3 analysis directory that the v4 pipeline does not reference.
gaps.impact: make_individual_figures.py reads from /Users/wangyanz/Desktop/Project/sequence_design/sequence_analysis_v3_0515/07.umap_vis/00.build_embeddings_model_embeddings/, not from sequence_analysis_v4_0621. The coordinates are a cached .npy that no script in the portal's stated data list regenerates, and there is no saved CSV of the coordinates.
gaps.workaround: Copy cca_winner_umap.npy and row_index.csv into the portal's versioned data snapshot at build time and record their source path and mtime (npy dated May 21, row_index May 21). Otherwise an interactive Fig 3c silently breaks if the v3 directory is ever cleaned up. Do not attempt to recompute the UMAP -- it would not reproduce the published figure.

gaps.gap: No per-nucleotide NTScore track is available in any of the enumerated data products.
gaps.impact: NTScore is the manuscript's core per-nucleotide quantity and the natural continuous background for the R1 sequence view, but the master table only carries per-motif aggregates (motif_score, motif_entropy, plddt). A reader who wants to see why a region was called cannot see the underlying score profile.
gaps.workaround: Ship the R1 view without a continuous track for v1 and render motifs as discrete highlighted segments only. If a score track is wanted later, it would need a separate export from the model; at 45.85 M positions across 18,093 transcripts, a uint8-quantized track would be roughly 46 MB raw before compression, so it should be sharded per transcript alongside the sequence shards rather than shipped whole.

gaps.gap: Nothing in the data marks which module edges are the ZNF/paralog-family artifacts that the manuscript explicitly corrects for, except in a hand-curated 30-row file.
gaps.impact: RAW_top30_annotated.csv carries the 'verdict' column naming artifacts such as 'ZNF clade artifact', but covers only 30 pairs out of 180,000. The portal must surface the statistical-co-occurrence caveat, and frac_co_ZNF plus n_indep_clades and n_indep_families are available per pair in protein_utr_FINAL_scores.csv, but there is no boolean artifact flag for the general case.
gaps.workaround: Expose frac_co_ZNF, n_indep_families, n_indep_clades and clade_concentration on every edge detail panel as first-class evidence columns, and show the 30 curated verdicts where they exist. Put the 'statistical co-occurrence, not demonstrated physical interaction' caveat in persistent UI chrome on the R3 view, not in a dismissible tooltip.

Per-column compressed sizes measured: motifs 9.01 MB, motif_score 5.57, unique_motif_id 5.35, motif_entropy 4.75, raw_motif_index 3.85, uniprot_annotations 2.96, MobIDB 1.85, plddt 1.82, interpro 1.44, motif_cluster 1.09, gene_symbol 0.46, sequence_id 0.44, region 0.004.

recommendations: Build a fully static, shard-based portal and do NOT use DuckDB-WASM. The measured comparison is decisive: a per-gene JSON shard answers R1 in 2.4 KB at the median (max 11.3 KB), while even an optimally re-partitioned parquet costs 0.21 MB per gene over HTTP range requests, and the parquet as it exists today costs 18.25 MB because it has one row group. Shards are ~90x cheaper than the best parquet case and ~7,700x cheaper than the current file, need no WASM runtime, no 3-5 s cold start, and no CORS/range-request server configuration. Total static payload is 114 MB gzipped with a 334 KB first paint.

Recommended deployment: option (a), a fully static site on GitHub Pages, with Zenodo as the citable archive. Concretely -- setup effort: ~1 day once the build script exists (push a directory, enable Pages); ongoing maintenance: effectively zero, no runtime to patch, no dependency CVEs, nothing to restart; cost: $0; survives the authors graduating: yes if the repo lives in a lab or institutional GitHub org rather than a personal account (move it before publication -- this is the single highest-risk item for long-term availability); URL stability: good under an org (username.github.io/repo or a custom lab domain), but a personal-account URL dies when the account is renamed or deleted; cold start: none, it is CDN-cached static files; data ceiling: 1 GB soft repo limit and 100 GB/month soft bandwidth, so 114 MB is comfortable. The one real friction is that ~36,700 small shard files make git clone slow -- mitigate by generating shards in CI from the source parquets rather than committing them, or by committing them to a separate data branch.

Rank the alternatives as follows, and pick one only if a stated requirement forces it. (b) static + DuckDB-WASM over hosted parquet: setup 3-5 days, needs the parquet rewritten sorted by gene_symbol at row_group_size=8000 (measured: 0.21 MB/gene, +24% file size), a server that honors HTTP Range, and a ~3-5 s WASM cold start; the only reason to choose it is arbitrary user-composed SQL across the full 889k rows, which none of R1/R2/R3 requires. (c) FastAPI/Flask + DuckDB on a lab VM: setup 2-3 days, gives 7.3 ms gene queries and arbitrary filtering, but adds a machine someone must patch, monitor and pay for; it dies quietly when the student leaves and the VM is reclaimed -- the worst outcome for a paper citation. (d) Streamlit/Dash/Panel/Shiny: fastest to a prototype (1-2 days) but the weakest fit here -- the framework owns the interaction model, so the custom sequence viewer and the force-directed network in R1/R3 fight it; free tiers sleep after inactivity giving 30+ s cold starts on a link from a paper, and a naive full-table load needs 782 MB RAM which will OOM ~1 GB tiers. (e) HuggingFace Spaces / Cloud Run: reasonable middle ground with a Docker image that pins the data, but free Spaces sleep (cold start 30 s+) and Cloud Run bills per request with no free-forever guarantee. Recommendation: static primary, and if interactive querying is later demanded, add (c) as an optional API behind the same static frontend rather than replacing it.

Rendering strategy, justified per view by measured scale. R1 sequence viewer: plain DOM/SVG with one span per motif-or-gap SEGMENT, not per nucleotide. Motifs never overlap within a (transcript, region) -- max interval depth is 1 across 4,000 sampled transcripts -- so a single flat track suffices with no stacking or interval tree. Segment counts are p50 89, p99 279, max 381 elements for a page showing all three sequences, versus p50 1,940 / max 7,784 for per-nucleotide spans. Render the sequence itself as plain text nodes inside those segment spans and draw the coordinate ruler as a separate SVG or canvas layer. R3 module network: SVG with d3-force. At 513 nodes / 1,860 edges (densest module M1 at 106 nodes / 774 edges) SVG keeps per-element hit-testing, CSS hover states and accessible focus for free, which the click-for-details requirement needs; canvas would force manual hit-testing for no benefit at this scale. Fig 3c UMAP: canvas (or WebGL if zoom/pan must stay at 60 fps). 180,000 points is far past SVG's practical ceiling -- an SVG circle per point would create 180,000 DOM nodes against a measured worst case of 381 elsewhere in the app. Use the 0.994 MB quantized typed-array payload and implement hover via a spatial index over the coordinate array rather than DOM events.

Reproducibility and citation: cut a versioned, immutable data snapshot and mint a Zenodo DOI for it before submission. Concretely -- (1) make the build script emit a manifest.json recording, for every input file, its absolute source path, size, mtime and SHA-256, plus a snapshot version like v1.0.0 and a build timestamp; this matters most for cca_winner_umap.npy, which lives in the v3 analysis tree that nothing else in the portal references and could be cleaned up without warning. (2) Deposit the generated static directory (114 MB, well inside Zenodo's 50 GB per-record limit) as a Zenodo record and cite the concept DOI in the manuscript, so the citation resolves even after the portal moves hosts. (3) Show 'Data snapshot v1.0.0, built YYYY-MM-DD' in persistent site chrome, not a footer, and link it to the DOI. (4) Make every view export what the reader is looking at: a Download CSV/JSON control on the gene motif table, the cluster member table, the module edge list and the GO table. Since each view is already backed by a discrete shard file, this is a client-side Blob download of data the browser already holds -- near-zero implementation cost, and it is what turns the portal from a figure viewer into a citable resource. (5) Pin duckdb and pyarrow versions in a requirements.txt committed alongside the build script, since duckdb is currently absent from every interpreter on this machine.

Surface the statistical caveat structurally, not as a disclaimer. Module membership is co-occurrence, not demonstrated physical interaction, and 45.3% of motif instances (402,908 of 889,215) belong to clusters with no module at all. Put the caveat in persistent chrome on the R3 view, render every edge detail panel with frac_co_ZNF, n_indep_families, n_indep_clades and clade_concentration as first-class columns beside the NPMI score, and give unassigned clusters real pages that state explicitly that they did not pass the phylogenetic-independence filter rather than hiding them. Show sub-threshold partners (passes_phylo_filter=false) greyed rather than omitting them, so a reader searching their favorite gene sees the actual evidence landscape instead of a curated subset.

Two data-correctness items the build must handle or the portal will be silently wrong. First, deduplicate the sequence table on refseq_id_without_ver before joining -- 1,296 RefSeq IDs are duplicated (NM_153443 appears 42 times mapped to 42 distinct ENSGs) and all duplicate groups were verified byte-identical in both utr3_sequence and protein_sequence, so dedup is lossless; skipping it inflates the join from the correct 18,093 to 20,481 and duplicates motif tracks in the R1 view. Second, treat plddt as a 0-1 scale (measured min 0.1, median 0.8, max 1.0), not the usual 0-100 AlphaFold scale, or every protein motif will render as 'very low confidence'; similarly motif_score is always negative (min -4.831, median -1.135, max -0.0), so color scales must be built for a negative domain. Use refseq_id_without_ver as the canonical join key -- it and best_refseq_mrna_id both cover 18,093/18,093, while transcript_stable_id covers 0.

Auto-derive cluster labels at build time instead of relying on the curated file. Only 37 of 900 clusters have a label in cluster_term_labels.csv and only 52 nodes appear in bipartite_nodes_all6.csv, so a network built from those files alone is mostly unlabelled node IDs. Compute a fallback label for every cluster from the master table -- top InterPro or UniProt term for protein clusters, top RBP by CLIP support for UTR clusters (203 distinct RBPs and 219 miRNA families across the data, both small enough to index client-side) -- and visually distinguish auto-derived labels from the 37 curated ones. Do the same for consensus: 449 of 900 clusters have no STREME string, so compute a PFM from member motif instances and render a logo client-side, labelled by provenance so the portal and the published figures never disagree silently.

recommendations: Do NOT parse table B's comma-joined strings. Concrete parsing rule: interpro_annotations -> never split, replace with overlapping_interpro_labels from processed/01.interpro/motif_interpro_annotations.parquet + interpro_entry_map.csv (comma-split is wrong for 41.34% of annotated protein motifs); uniprot_annotations -> never split, recompute typed features from processed/03.uniprot/uniprot_annotation.parquet (comma-split is wrong for 6.894%); elm_annotations -> never split, re-join elm_instances.tsv (fragments like 'TRAF2 group (TRAF1' / '2' / '3' prove breakage); idpo_annotations -> safe, split on ';' (not ','); signalp_annotation -> safe, only 2 possible values. Keep the original joined string in the record as `*_legacy_string` for provenance but never render it as chips.

Build a single portal-side 'annotation build' script (one pass, ~5 minutes on this machine with /opt/anaconda3/envs/bio/bin/python) that reproduces table B keyed on raw_motif_index but ID-bearing and region-correct: (1) start from identified_motifs_with_clusters.0513.parquet (keeps kmeans_label, which table B dropped); (2) left-join interpro labels, idpo_ids, mobidb Entry; (3) recompute UniProt features with type+coords using the 0-based-corrected overlap rule; (4) apply region=='protein' masks to MobiDB/IDPO/SignalP; (5) attach RBP peak aggregates from motif_rbp_overlaps.parquet; (6) emit per-region parquet shards plus a small per-gene JSON cache. Everything is local; no network calls except the already-done MyGene symbol mapping.

Show provenance and rules in the UI, not just values. Each annotation chip should carry (a) its source database, (b) the overlap rule used ('motif overlaps feature' for InterPro/UniProt/ELM vs 'motif contained in region' for MobiDB/IDPO), (c) the evidence count where available (CLIP peaks, cell lines), and (d) an FDR when it comes from the cluster-level table. This is what makes the portal defensible next to the manuscript's own caveat that module membership is statistical co-occurrence, not demonstrated physical interaction.
